clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive demyelinating Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy caused by mutations in PRX, the gene encoding periaxin, a Schwann cell protein essential for myelin sheath stabilisation.
Onset is usually in infancy or early childhood with delayed walking, and the phenotype can resemble Dejerine-Sottas disease.
A hallmark is disproportionately prominent sensory involvement, with sensory ataxia and large-fibre sensory loss dominating the picture.
Motor nerve conduction velocities are markedly slowed, reflecting severe demyelination.
Skeletal complications such as pes cavus and progressive scoliosis are common and contribute substantially to disability.
Nerve biopsy shows demyelination with onion-bulb formation and focally folded myelin.
Periaxin is part of the dystroglycan-DRP2-periaxin complex that links the Schwann cell to its basal lamina, and its loss destabilises the myelin sheath.
Despite early and sometimes severe onset, progression is often relatively slow so that ambulation may be retained for many years.
reference.pathophysiology: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 4F is an autosomal recessive demyelinating neuropathy caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in PRX (chromosome 19), which encodes periaxin. Periaxin exists as two isoforms in myelinating Schwann cells and, through its PDZ domain, forms part of the dystroglycan-DRP2-periaxin (DRP2) complex that anchors the abaxonal Schwann cell membrane to the surrounding basal lamina. This scaffold is required for the mechanical stabilisation and normal elongation of the myelin sheath and for the formation of Cajal bands. Loss of functional periaxin destabilises myelin, producing a severe demyelinating neuropathy with recurrent demyelination and remyelination that gives rise to onion-bulb formations and focally folded myelin on biopsy. The disproportionate large-fibre sensory dysfunction and sensory ataxia that characterise CMT4F reflect the particular vulnerability of heavily myelinated sensory fibres to this Schwann cell adhesion defect.
additionalDifferentials: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 4H (FGD4), another recessive demyelinating childhood-onset CMT

Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 4B1/4B2 (MTMR2/SBF2) with myelin outfoldings
Dejerine-Sottas disease and congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy
Demyelinating CMT1 caused by PMP22 or MPZ mutations
Acquired chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy in childhood
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies demonstrating markedly slowed motor velocities consistent with severe demyelination
PRX sequencing or a hereditary neuropathy gene panel to confirm biallelic mutations
Nerve biopsy in atypical cases, showing onion bulbs, demyelination and focally folded myelin
Spinal imaging and orthopaedic review to monitor scoliosis
Detailed sensory and proprioceptive testing to document the prominent sensory ataxia
Three-generation pedigree and enquiry into consanguinity given recessive inheritance
redFlags: Severe or rapidly worsening sensory ataxia impairing balance and safe mobility
Rapidly progressive scoliosis threatening respiratory function or requiring surgical intervention
Emergence of respiratory or bulbar symptoms, which are uncommon and warrant reassessment
Any subacute deterioration suggesting a superimposed acquired inflammatory neuropathy
reference.prognosis: CMT4F begins early and can be clinically severe, but progression is frequently slow, so that many affected individuals retain ambulation into adulthood; long-term disability is driven mainly by sensory ataxia and skeletal deformity such as scoliosis.
pitfalls: The striking sensory ataxia may be misattributed to a cerebellar or dorsal-column disorder rather than a demyelinating neuropathy.
The Dejerine-Sottas-like severity can be wrongly assumed to indicate a poor motor outcome despite the often slow progression.
Recessive inheritance means the family history is frequently unremarkable, which should not deter genetic testing.
Focally folded myelin on biopsy overlaps with other recessive demyelinating subtypes, so genetic confirmation is required.
references: Peripheral and hereditary neuropathy reference texts
management: No disease-specific pharmacotherapy; supportive and rehabilitative care through a neuromuscular multidisciplinary team
Physiotherapy with balance and gait rehabilitation and mobility aids for the prominent sensory ataxia
Ankle-foot orthoses and podiatry for foot deformity and pes cavus
Orthopaedic and spinal management of progressive scoliosis
Neuropathic pain management with gabapentinoids or tricyclic agents
Avoidance of neurotoxic drugs such as vincristine
Autosomal recessive genetic counselling with carrier testing and family screening, guided by consanguinity
